items.title: Why a 660-ton ball makes Taipei 101 safer
items.summary: Why does Taipei 101 hang a 660-ton ball near the top? The ball is 5.5 meters across, built from 41 layers of steel plate, each 12.5 centimeters thick, and the official site puts it at 660 metric tons. It hangs on cables, and when wind pushes the tower one way, the ball swings against it. That's called a tuned mass damper. The official site says its main purpose is to reduce the swaying of the tower during strong winds. Same weight, but free to swing, it protects the building. Idea and structure: Mark Rober's Short "How To Keep a Skyscraper From Falling Over". Sources are in the pinned comment. Photos: Wpcpey (CC BY 4.0), Chaplain iMonk and Richard Bitting (CC BY 2.0), via Wikimedia Commons. Footage: NASA #shorts #science #engineering

items.title: How fighter pilots stay awake at 9 g
items.summary: How does a fighter pilot stay awake at 9 g? At 5 g, a 2016 study on rats measured the blood pressure in the head falling by about 80 mmHg, to nearly zero. No pressure, no blood to the brain, so the vision goes, then the pilot does. The pilot breathes out hard against a closed throat for 3 to 4 seconds, which squeezes the chest and pushes blood pressure back up. A 2026 review says doing the full straining maneuver right adds about 4 g. The limit for military jets is still about 9 g, and that limit is the pilot, not the plane. Idea and structure: Mark Rober's Short "Why Do People Pass Out On Roller Coasters?" Sources are in the pinned comment. #shorts #science #aviation
